clinicalPearls: AIVR is a wide-complex ventricular rhythm at a rate of roughly 40 to 120 per minute, faster than the intrinsic ventricular escape rate but slower than ventricular tachycardia.
It is the classic and generally benign marker of successful reperfusion following thrombolysis or primary percutaneous intervention in acute myocardial infarction.
The rhythm typically emerges when sinus rate slows and the enhanced ventricular focus overtakes it, and it recedes as sinus rate recovers.
Onset and offset are gradual, and fusion and capture beats are common at the transitions as the two competing pacemakers interact.
It is usually haemodynamically well tolerated and self-limiting, so suppression is rarely required.
Loss of atrioventricular synchrony can occasionally reduce cardiac output in patients dependent on the atrial contribution to filling.
Other associations include digoxin toxicity, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, cocaine use and the postoperative cardiac surgical setting.
If treatment is needed to restore atrioventricular synchrony, accelerating the sinus rate to overdrive the ectopic focus is preferred over suppressive antiarrhythmics.
reference.pathophysiology: AIVR arises from enhanced automaticity of a subsidiary pacemaker within the His-Purkinje system or ventricular myocardium. The abnormal focus discharges faster than its intrinsic escape rate but not fast enough to constitute ventricular tachycardia. Because the focus and the sinus node compete, the ventricular rhythm typically manifests only when it transiently exceeds the sinus rate, such as during sinus slowing or atrioventricular block, and yields to sinus rhythm when the sinus rate rises. In the setting of reperfusion, washout of ischaemic metabolites and calcium loading of injured Purkinje tissue is thought to heighten automaticity. The competing pacemakers frequently generate fusion and capture complexes at onset and termination.
additionalDifferentials: supraventricular rhythm with bundle branch block
ventricular escape rhythm in complete heart block
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG to confirm rate and identify fusion and capture beats
continuous telemetry to document onset, offset and relationship to sinus rate
serial cardiac troponin and ECG in the context of suspected reperfusion
serum electrolytes including potassium and magnesium
serum digoxin concentration when toxicity is suspected
echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural disease
redFlags: haemodynamic compromise attributable to loss of atrioventricular synchrony
acceleration into sustained rapid ventricular tachycardia
occurrence with digoxin toxicity requiring specific management
features suggesting active ischaemia rather than reperfusion
reference.prognosis: AIVR is generally benign, transient and self-limiting, particularly as a reperfusion phenomenon, and rarely requires specific therapy. Prognosis is dominated by the underlying condition rather than the rhythm itself.
pitfalls: Misclassifying AIVR as ventricular tachycardia and administering unnecessary or harmful suppressive treatment.
Attempting to suppress a benign, self-limiting rhythm rather than supporting sinus rate if symptomatic.
Overlooking digoxin toxicity or electrolyte disturbance as a cause outside the reperfusion setting.
Assuming reperfusion is complete solely on the basis of AIVR without corroborating clinical and angiographic data.
Failing to recognise loss of atrioventricular synchrony as the mechanism of intolerance in filling-dependent patients.
